response.text:
Ere the English ship fades from sight, be it set down that she hailed from London and bore the name of Samuel Enderby, original of that famous whaling house; a house which, in a whaleman’s account, comes not far behind Tudors and Bourbons for historical interest. Long before 1775 our valiant Coffins and Maceys of Nantucket and the Vineyard had pursued the Sperm Whale in Atlantic waters; but in 1775 Enderby & Sons fitted the first regular English sperm-cruisers. Be it distinctly recorded, that the Nantucketers were the first among mankind to harpoon with civilized steel the great Sperm Whale; and for half a century they alone so harpooned him.

In 1778 the Amelia, sent by the vigorous Enderbys, boldly rounded Cape Horn, first to lower in the great South Sea; her lucky hold full of sperm opened the Pacific grounds to English and Americans. Then the Rattler, a sloop-of-war, was sent whaling by British inducement—how much she did, who knows? In 1819 their discovery-ship Syren tasted the remote waters of Japan; commanded by Captain Coffin of Nantucket, she made known that great ground.

All honor to the Enderbies, therefore, whose house, I think, exists to the present day; though doubtless the original Samuel must long ago have slipped his cable for the great South Sea of the other world.

The ship named after him was worthy of the honor, being a very fast sailer and a noble craft every way. I boarded her once at midnight somewhere off the Patagonian coast, and drank good flip down in the forecastle. It was a fine gam we had, and they were all trumps—every soul on board. A short life to them, and a jolly death. And that fine gam I had—long, very long after old Ahab touched her planks with his ivory heel—it minds me of the noble, solid, Saxon hospitality of that ship; and may my parson forget me, and the devil remember me, if I ever lose sight of it. Flip? Did I say we had flip? Yes, and we flipped it at the rate of ten gallons the hour; and when the squall came (for it’s squally off there by Patagonia), and all hands—visitors and all—were called to reef topsails, we were so top-heavy that we had to swing each other aloft in bowlines; and we ignorantly furled the skirts of our jackets into the sails, so that we hung there, reefed fast in the howling gale, a warning to drunken tars. Down again—so sober we had to pass the flip once more, though the savage spray pickled it. The beef was tough, with body in it; some swore it bull, others dromedary. Dumplings—small, globular, indestructible—seemed to roll within you like billiard-balls; the bread was anti-scorbutic and best eaten in a dark corner. All in all, the Samuel Enderby was a jolly ship: good fare and plenty; crack fellows all.

Why such abounding good cheer in certain English whalers? The English merchant-ship scrimps; not so the English whaler. Preceded in the fishery by the Hollanders and their kin, from whom they derived not only many terms still extant but their fat old fashions touching plenty to eat and drink, the English good cheer is incidental and particular, and therefore must have some special origin. During my researches in the Leviathanic histories, I stumbled upon an ancient Dutch volume, the “Dan Coopman,” by one Fitz Swackhammer. But my friend Dr. Snodhead, a very learned man, professor of Low Dutch and High German in the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott’s, to whom I handed the work for translation, giving him a box of sperm candles for his trouble, assured me that “Dan Coopman” did not mean “The Cooper,” but “The Merchant.” In its chapter “Smeer,” or “Fat,” I found a list of the outfits for the larders and cellars of 180 sail of Dutch whalemen, from which I transcribe: 400,000 lbs. beef; 60,000 lbs. Friesland pork; 150,000 lbs. stock-fish; 550,000 lbs. biscuit; 72,000 lbs. soft bread; 2,800 firkins butter; 20,000 lbs. Texel & Leyden cheese; 144,000 lbs. inferior cheese; 550 ankers Geneva; 10,800 barrels beer. Most statistical tables are parchingly dry in the reading; not so in the present case, however, where the reader is flooded with whole pipes, barrels, quarts, and gills of good gin and good cheer. At the time, I devoted three days to the studious digesting of all this beer, beef, and bread, during which many profound thoughts were incidentally suggested to me, capable of a transcendental and Platonic application; and, furthermore, I compiled supplementary tables of my own, touching the probable quantity of stock-fish, etc., consumed by every Low Dutch harpooneer in that ancient Greenland and Spitzbergen whale fishery. In the first place, the amount of butter, and Texel and Leyden cheese consumed, seems amazing. I impute it, though, to their naturally unctuous natures, being rendered still more unctuous by the nature of their vocation, and especially by their pursuing their game in those frigid Polar Seas, on the very coasts of that Esquimaux country where the convivial natives pledge each other in bumpers of train oil. The quantity of beer, too, is very large, 10,800 barrels; and reckoning thirty men to a ship, for a three months’ cruise, that is two barrels of beer per man, exclusive of his fair proportion of that 550 ankers of gin. High livers, those Hollanders; and the English have not neglected so excellent an example. For say they: when cruising in an empty ship, if you can get nothing better out of the world, get a good dinner out of it, at least. And this empties the decanter.
